summary: Experiments with the eyeless Mexican cavefish (Astyanax mexicanus) suggest a ketogenic diet can reduce autism-like behaviors. Cavefish are asocial and swim in repetitive circles, but after a month on ketogenic milk they began to follow each other and stopped circling, like social surface fish. Researchers suspect the dopaminergic system is the diet's target, and they are probing mitochondrial and epigenetic mechanisms.
one_line: A ketogenic diet made asocial, repetitive-swimming Mexican cavefish behave more socially, hinting at dopamine-related mechanisms relevant to autism treatment.
key_facts: The ketogenic diet is high in protein and fat but low in carbs and induces ketosis, in which the body burns fat and produces ketones.
Children with epilepsy are sometimes placed on the ketogenic diet because it helps reduce seizure frequency.
The study was published in BMC Biology in 2023 and used the Mexican cavefish, Astyanax mexicanus.
Cavefish avoid their peers and engage in repetitive behavior such as swimming in circles, which Masato Yoshizawa noticed resembled autism in patients.
Cavefish gene regulation patterns also resembled those of autistic patients, according to Yoshizawa.
Ryan Lee, a physician at Shriners Hospital for Children Honolulu, said the cavefish video looked very similar to what he observes in his patients.
Cavefish were fed the same ketogenic milk given to human patients, with modifications for fish, and compared with river-dwelling surface fish of the same species.
Surface fish follow and swim together and do not swim in circles, whereas cavefish rarely show social following.
After a month on the ketogenic diet, cavefish followed each other in groups and stopped going round in circles.
Attention to a specific task and sleeping were unaffected by the diet in cavefish.
Yoshizawa suspects the target of the ketogenic diet is the dopaminergic system.
Two plausible mechanisms for how ketones affect behavior involve mitochondria and epigenetics.
Cavefish are not an exact model for human autism, but the work could help identify better pathways or a more efficient specific ketone for treatment.
The article was corrected on November 2, 2023 to state Ryan Lee works at Shriners Hospital for Children Honolulu, not the University of Hawai‘i Mānoa.
